objective.statement: Name compound intervals, larger than an octave, in either of the two accepted ways.
successCriteria: I count letter names beyond 8 for the number.
I know an octave and a 5th is a 12th, not a 13th.
I know the quality does not change when I use the compound name.

explanation.text: An interval larger than an octave is a compound interval. Its number goes on counting past 8 in the same way: 9th, 10th, 11th, up to the 15th (two octaves). Count the letter names from the lower note to the upper note, counting both ends.

music.textAlternative: Two semibreves: middle C, then the G an octave and a fifth above it.

explanation.caption: C up to the G above: a perfect 12th.

explanation.text: There is a trap. It is tempting to say 'an octave and a 5th' means 8 + 5 = 13. But the octave and the 5th share a note, so the number is 7 + 5 = 12: a 12th. To turn a simple interval into a compound one, add 7; to go back, subtract 7.

There is another way to number a compound interval: keep the number it would have inside the lower octave and add the word compound. A major 10th is a compound major 3rd; a perfect 12th is a compound perfect 5th; an augmented 11th is a compound augmented 4th. Both ways are accepted, and the quality is the same in each.
Compound number = simple number + 7. The quality never changes: a major 3rd becomes a major 10th.

music.textAlternative: Two semibreves: E then G sharp an octave and a third above.

steps: Count: E to G is a 3rd inside the octave.
E to G♯ is major: a major 10th (or compound major 3rd).
demonstration.textAlternative: E up to the G sharp above the octave: a major 10th.

guided.prompt: An octave and a 3rd above the lower note: what is the number of the whole interval?

3.reason: That is the simple interval inside the octave; the whole interval is larger than an octave.

9.reason: Count up from the lower note: an octave is the 8th note, and the 3rd above that note is further on.

11.reason: Adding 8 + 3 counts the shared note twice. An octave is 7 steps on top of the lower note, so 3 + 7 = 10.

hints: Add 7 to the number of the simple interval, because the octave and the interval share a note.

mistakes.counted-one-end-only: Count both notes: the bottom note is 1, then every letter name up to and including the top note.
mistakes.quality-from-wrong-key: Judge the quality by imagining the major scale on the lower note. Is the top note in it?
mistakes.compound-arithmetic: An octave and a 5th is a 12th: add 7, not 8.
mistakes.enharmonic-spelling: That sounds right, but intervals depend on letter names. Check how many letter names the interval spans.
mistakes.augmented-diminished-swap: Is the interval a semitone bigger or smaller than the major/perfect version? Bigger means augmented; smaller means diminished (or minor).

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Count the letter names first, then compare with the major scale on the lower note.
